# Regression: interactions and non-linear associations

```{r}
#| label: setup-14
#| include: false
Sys.setlocale("LC_CTYPE", "en_US.UTF-8")
options(width = 78)
fmt <- function(x, digits = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits)
```

Everything so far has assumed two things about a regression, and both are often wrong.

The first is that each predictor has **the same effect for everybody**. The second is that the relationship is a **straight line**. This session relaxes them one at a time.

```{r}
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(psych)
library(ggeffects)

swe <- readRDS("data/swe.rds")

trust_items <- c(
  "tr_parl", "tr_govt", "tr_court",
  "tr_sci", "tr_party", "tr_media"
)
swe$trust <- fa(swe[, trust_items], nfactors = 1, fm = "ml")$scores[, 1]

swe$sex <- factor(
  swe$female,
  levels = c(0, 1),
  labels = c("Men", "Women")
)
```

## Interactions

In session 11 we found that trust in institutions predicts how democratic people think Sweden is, and that it does so about equally on both sides of the political divide once you control for it.

But "controlling for" and "the same for everybody" are different claims. A model with `trust + bloc` says the trust slope is identical for left and right voters, and forces it to be. An **interaction** lets it differ.

```{r}
model_int <- lm(demlevel ~ trust * bloc, data = swe)

round(coef(summary(model_int)), 3)
```

`trust * bloc` is shorthand. It puts in `trust`, `bloc`, and the product of the two — the interaction term, printed as `trust:blocRight`. You could write `trust + bloc + trust:bloc` and get the same model.

### Reading it

Four numbers, and the trap is in the middle two.

**`(Intercept)` = `r fmt(coef(model_int)[1])`** — predicted rating for a left-bloc voter with average trust.

**`trust` = `r fmt(coef(model_int)[2])`** — the trust slope **for left-bloc voters only**. Not for everyone. Not on average.

**`blocRight` = `r fmt(coef(model_int)[3])`** — the bloc difference **at trust = 0**. Not overall.

**`trust:blocRight` = `r fmt(coef(model_int)[4])`** — how much the trust slope *changes* for right-bloc voters. So their slope is `r fmt(coef(model_int)[2])` + `r fmt(coef(model_int)[4])` = `r fmt(coef(model_int)[2] + coef(model_int)[4])`.

> **Once you add an interaction, the other two coefficients change meaning.** They are no longer average effects. They are the effect of one variable *when the other is zero*, which is why it matters enormously whether zero is a meaningful value.
>
> Here it happens to be fine, because `trust` is a factor score, so zero is the average. Had we used raw age, `blocRight` would have been the bloc difference among newborns.

The interaction is significant (*p* = `r fmt(coef(summary(model_int))[4, 4], 3)`), so trust does more work for right-bloc voters than for left-bloc voters: `r fmt(coef(model_int)[2] + coef(model_int)[4])` points per unit of trust against `r fmt(coef(model_int)[2])`.

### Plot it, always

Interaction coefficients are close to unreadable in a table. Nobody should have to do that arithmetic in their head, and the sign of an interaction term tells you almost nothing on its own.

```{r}
#| label: fig-int
#| fig-height: 3.6
predictions <- predict_response(
  model_int,
  terms = c("trust [-2:2 by=0.5]", "bloc")
)

plot(predictions) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(end = 0.7) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(end = 0.7) +
  labs(
    x = "Trust in institutions (factor score)",
    y = "Predicted rating of Swedish democracy",
    colour = "Bloc",
    fill = "Bloc",
    title = NULL
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

Giving `terms` two variables produces one line per group of the second, and `scale_colour_viridis_d()` and `scale_fill_viridis_d()` put the two lines on the colourblind-safe palette from session 4. Now the interaction is obvious: two lines that are not parallel, and that **cross**.

Read what it says. Among people who distrust institutions, left-bloc voters rate Swedish democracy *higher* than right-bloc voters. Among people who trust institutions, it is the other way round. The lines meet at a trust score of about `r fmt(-coef(model_int)[3] / coef(model_int)[4])`.

So the answer to "is there a winner–loser gap?" is: it depends who you ask. That is what an interaction means, and no single coefficient could have said it.

**Non-parallel lines are what an interaction is.** If you cannot see it on this plot, it is not there in any meaningful sense, whatever the p-value says.

Note also the top right corner: the model predicts `r fmt(max(as.data.frame(predictions)$predicted))` for the most trusting right-bloc voters, on a scale that stops at 10. Session 12 again, and one more reason not to read predictions at the edges too literally.

### When the main effect misleads

A second example, because this catches people.

```{r}
model_age <- lm(lr_self ~ age * sex, data = swe)

round(coef(summary(model_age)), 4)
```

The coefficient on `age` is `r fmt(coef(model_age)[2], 4)` with *p* = `r fmt(coef(summary(model_age))[2, 4], 3)` — nothing. Read carelessly, that says age does not matter.

It says no such thing. It says age does not matter **for men**, since men are the reference category. For women the slope is `r fmt(coef(model_age)[2], 4)` + `r fmt(coef(model_age)[4], 4)` = `r fmt(coef(model_age)[2] + coef(model_age)[4], 4)` — positive, and the interaction is significant at *p* = `r fmt(coef(summary(model_age))[4, 4], 3)`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-int2
#| fig-height: 3.4
age_predictions <- predict_response(model_age, terms = c("age", "sex"))

plot(age_predictions) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(end = 0.7) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(end = 0.7) +
  labs(
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Predicted left-right self-placement",
    colour = "Sex",
    fill = "Sex",
    title = NULL
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

Older women place themselves further right than younger women; among men, age makes little difference. Two groups, two different stories, and a model without the interaction would have averaged them into one weak effect.

::: {.discussion}
**A question.** In `model_age`, swapping the reference category from men to women would change the coefficient on `age` from `r fmt(coef(model_age)[2], 4)` to `r fmt(coef(model_age)[2] + coef(model_age)[4], 4)`, and its p-value from non-significant to significant.

Nothing about the data has changed. What does that tell you about reporting "the effect of age" from a model containing an interaction?
:::

> **Do not go hunting.** With ten predictors there are forty-five possible two-way interactions, and at the conventional threshold you would expect a couple to come out significant by chance alone. Test interactions you have a reason to expect. An interaction found by searching needs replicating before it means anything.

## Non-linear relationships

The second assumption. Sometimes the relationship is not a straight line at all — and session 5 gave us a case where it *cannot* be.

```{r}
world <- readr::read_csv("data/world.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
world <- world |> filter(!is.na(gdp), !is.na(life))

world$gdp_k <- world$gdp / 1000
```

`gdp_k` is income per head in **thousands** of dollars. One dollar more or less makes no visible difference to anything, so the coefficient on it would be a number like 0.0002. Changing the unit changes how the coefficient reads and nothing else.

Income has a floor at zero and no ceiling. Life expectancy has both. We argued in session 5 that this rules out a straight line, because a line rising forever eventually promises impossible lifespans.

Fit one anyway and see.

```{r}
linear <- lm(life ~ gdp_k, data = world)

summary(linear)
```

Each thousand dollars more goes with `r fmt(coef(linear)[2])` more years of life expectancy. The coefficient is clearly significant, and adjusted R² is `r fmt(summary(linear)$adj.r.squared, 3)`. Nothing in that output says anything is wrong.

Now ask it to predict.

```{r}
extremes <- data.frame(gdp_k = c(1, 50, 150, 300))
extremes$linear <- predict(linear, newdata = extremes)

round(extremes, 1)
```

A life expectancy of `r fmt(predict(linear, newdata = data.frame(gdp_k = 300)), 0)` years in the last row. The model is not confused — it is doing exactly what a straight line does. The mistake was ours, in fitting one.

### A squared term

To let the line bend, add the **square** of the predictor as a second predictor. The model can then bend once: up and then down, or down and then up. This is called a **quadratic** model.

$$\text{life} = b_0 + b_1 \times \text{income} + b_2 \times \text{income}^2$$

```{r}
quadratic <- lm(life ~ gdp_k + I(gdp_k^2), data = world)

summary(quadratic)
```

`I()` is needed around `gdp_k^2`. Inside a formula `^` means something else — interactions to a given order — and `I()` says "treat this as ordinary arithmetic".

The squared term is clearly significant, which says that the relationship is **not a straight line**. Adjusted R² rises from `r fmt(summary(linear)$adj.r.squared, 3)` to `r fmt(summary(quadratic)$adj.r.squared, 3)`. The adjusted version is the one to compare, because the second model has one more term.

```{r}
#| label: fig-nonlin
#| fig-height: 3.8
ggplot(world, aes(x = gdp_k, y = life)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    formula = y ~ x,
    se = FALSE,
    colour = "grey50",
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    formula = y ~ x + I(x^2),
    se = FALSE,
    colour = "black"
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(40, 100)) +
  labs(
    x = "GDP per capita (thousands of PPP dollars)",
    y = "Life expectancy at birth (years)"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

The dashed line is the straight fit and the solid one the quadratic. The straight line is too **high** at both ends and too **low** in the middle — the signature of fitting a line to a curve, and exactly what the residual plot in session 11 was looking for.

### Reading it

A squared term is like an interaction: the two coefficients **cannot be read separately**. "One more unit of income, holding income squared constant" is not something that can happen. Read them together.

**The signs give the shape.** The first coefficient is positive (`r fmt(coef(quadratic)[2], 3)`) and the squared one is negative (`r fmt(coef(quadratic)[3], 4)`): the curve rises, and rises less and less. Had the signs been the other way round, it would fall first and then rise.

**Predictions give the size.** There is no single effect of income any more, so predict at several values, equally far apart.

```{r}
steps <- data.frame(gdp_k = c(5, 15, 50, 60))
steps$predicted <- predict(quadratic, newdata = steps)

round(steps, 1)
```

Going from 5,000 to 15,000 dollars goes with about `r fmt(predict(quadratic, data.frame(gdp_k = 15)) - predict(quadratic, data.frame(gdp_k = 5)), 1)` more years. Going from 50,000 to 60,000 — the same 10,000 — goes with `r fmt(predict(quadratic, data.frame(gdp_k = 60)) - predict(quadratic, data.frame(gdp_k = 50)), 1)`.

**The turning point says where it stops rising.** It is minus the first coefficient divided by twice the second.

```{r}
b <- coef(quadratic)

-b[2] / (2 * b[3])
```

About `r fmt(-coef(quadratic)[2] / (2 * coef(quadratic)[3]), 0)` thousand dollars. Always check where that is in the data. Here only `r sum(world$gdp_k > -coef(quadratic)[2] / (2 * coef(quadratic)[3]))` of the `r nrow(world)` countries are richer than that.

### Where not to trust it

A quadratic always turns round eventually, whether or not the world does.

```{r}
extremes$quadratic <- predict(quadratic, newdata = extremes)

round(extremes, 1)
```

At 300,000 dollars the straight line says `r fmt(predict(linear, newdata = data.frame(gdp_k = 300)), 0)` years and the quadratic says `r fmt(predict(quadratic, newdata = data.frame(gdp_k = 300)), 0)`. Both are impossible. The richest country in the data is at `r fmt(max(world$gdp_k), 0)` thousand, and beyond that neither model knows anything.

So use the quadratic to describe the relationship **where the data are**: steep among poor countries, nearly flat among rich ones. The bend downwards at the far right is how a quadratic is built, and it rests on a couple of countries. It is not a finding that life expectancy falls when countries get very rich.

**Have a reason for the curve.** A squared term belongs in a model when there is an argument for a bend — session 5's limits, or a relationship that rises and then falls, such as income over the life course. Adding squared terms to see what becomes significant is hunting, just as it is with interactions.

::: {.discussion}
**A question.** The quadratic turns down at about `r fmt(-coef(quadratic)[2] / (2 * coef(quadratic)[3]), 0)` thousand dollars per head.

What would you need to see in the data before you believed that life expectancy really falls beyond that point?
:::

::: {.reporting}
**How to write it up.**

An interaction:

> The association between trust and evaluations of democracy differed by bloc (b = `r fmt(coef(model_int)[4])`, SE = `r fmt(coef(summary(model_int))[4, 2])`, *p* = `r fmt(coef(summary(model_int))[4, 4], 3)`). Among left-bloc voters a one-unit increase in the trust score corresponded to a `r fmt(coef(model_int)[2])`-point higher rating; among right-bloc voters, `r fmt(coef(model_int)[2] + coef(model_int)[4])` points (Figure 1).

A curve:

> Life expectancy was modelled as a quadratic function of GDP per capita, since a bounded outcome cannot keep rising in a straight line. The squared term was negative and significant (b = `r fmt(coef(quadratic)[3], 4)`, SE = `r fmt(coef(summary(quadratic))[3, 2], 4)`, *p* < .001; income in thousands of dollars): the association is steep among poor countries and nearly flat among rich ones. An additional 10,000 dollars per head corresponded to `r fmt(predict(quadratic, data.frame(gdp_k = 15)) - predict(quadratic, data.frame(gdp_k = 5)), 1)` more years of life expectancy at 5,000 dollars, but only `r fmt(predict(quadratic, data.frame(gdp_k = 60)) - predict(quadratic, data.frame(gdp_k = 50)), 1)` at 50,000 (adjusted R² = `r fmt(summary(quadratic)$adj.r.squared, 2)`, *n* = `r nobs(quadratic)`; Figure 2).

Mistakes to avoid:

- **Reporting an interaction without a plot.** The coefficients are not readable on their own.
- **Interpreting a main effect as an average effect** when an interaction is in the model. It is the effect when the other variable is zero.
- **Reporting a main effect's p-value** from a model with an interaction, as though it meant something general. It depends on the reference category.
- **Fishing for interactions.** Test the ones you predicted.
- **Adding a squared term only because it raises R².** The shape should follow from what the variables are.
- **Reading the two coefficients of a quadratic separately.** Give predicted values, or a plot.
- **Not checking where the turning point is.** It may lie outside the data, or rest on a handful of cases.
- **Extrapolating a quadratic**, which always turns round in the end.
:::
